newsitem.title: USA: ALPINE SKIING-NEW MEN'S DOWNHILL FOR 1999 WORLD CHAMPIONSHIPS.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-NEW MEN'S DOWNHILL FOR 1999 WORLD CHAMPIONSHIPS.

text.p: Stung by criticism of the International downhill course on Vail Mountain, organisers unveiled plans Wednesday for a new downhill to be carved out of Beaver Creek Resort in time for the 1999 world championships.

Former Olympic champion Bernhard Russi, the downhill technical advisor for the International Ski Federation (FIS), is overseeing the design and construction of the new "Birds of Prey" course, to be used for the men's downhill.

"The goal for this downhill is to find a challenging course that will identify the best skier in the world at the world championships," said Russi. "The public on course and watching on TV should feel the excitement and difficulty of our sport.
"I think we have done it with Birds of Prey."

The course is set high on the mountain with the start at an elevation of 11,424 feet (3,482-meters) and will finish at the bottom of Red Tail at 8,964 feet (2,732 meters). Spectators will use lifts and shuttle buses to reach the finish area.

The vertical drop of the course will be 2,460 feet (750 meters) with an average gradient of 27 percent, increasing to 45 percent in sections. Skiers should average about 60 miles per hour (100 kph) and reach top speeds of 90 mph (150 kph).
"There are four parts to the course," said Russi. "The first part is flat for about 400 yards (meters). After that, it's over. The rest is a fight.
"The next section will be a fight against speed. We have to put three or four turns in, and quite tight ones, to control speed.
"The next quarter gets faster and faster and the last quarter is what we all like about downhill -- flying. There are lots of jumps and every one is different."
Russi said the view from the finish was "spectacular" and that fans would be able to follow the race for 30 to 50 seconds.

The course may be considered somewhat short and the winning time figures to be between 1:35 and 1:40, but Russi felt confident it would become the preeminent downhill in the United States and among the best in the world.
"Birds of Prey will be counted as one of the most modern and demanding courses in the world," he said.
Organisers plan to stage a World Cup downhill and a Super-G test event in early December next season.
